items.h1: How to blur background on iPhone (after you already took the photo)
items.answer: To blur the background on iPhone after the photo is taken, open it in How to Blur Photo, keep the Background tab selected so the subject is detected automatically, choose Gaussian, drag Radius until the background is as soft as you want, and tap Save. It works on any photo in your library, not only Portrait shots, and processing stays on your iPhone.
items.intro: Most answers to “how to blur background on iPhone” send you to Portrait mode. That is fine if you have not taken the picture yet. If the photo is already in Recents, shot in normal Photo mode, on a front camera, or sent to you by someone else, Portrait mode cannot help. This guide covers what the built-in Photos app can and cannot do, then the exact taps to blur the background of an existing photo.
items.image_alt: Background tab selected in How to Blur Photo with the subject sharp and the wall behind her blurred

native.heading: What iPhone can do on its own
paragraphs: Portrait mode records depth information at the moment you press the shutter. Later, in Photos → Edit, you can change the f-number to make that background blur stronger or weaker. That only works on photos that were captured in Portrait mode in the first place. A regular Photo-mode picture has no depth map, so the f-number slider is simply not there.

Markup can draw over a background, and the Clean Up tool on Apple Intelligence iPhones can remove objects, but neither of them produces a photographic blur. If you want a sharp subject in front of a soft background on a photo you already have, you need an editor that separates the subject itself.

sections.heading: Why an after-the-fact blur app is the practical fix
paragraphs: How to Blur Photo (the app behind Make Blur) detects the person or object in the frame, keeps it sharp, and applies the blur only to what is behind it. You control the strength with a Radius slider, so a portrait can get a gentle depth-of-field look and a busy street shot can get a heavy one.

It is free to download from the App Store, needs iPhone with iOS 18.6 or later, and processes everything on the device. Basic background blur is included; extra styles and tools are optional in-app purchases.

sections.heading: Picking the right strength
paragraphs: A Radius around 30–45 looks like a wide-aperture lens: the background is soft but still readable. Around 60–80 the background turns into colour and shape only, which is what most people mean by “blurry background” on social posts. Anything above 90 is a stylistic choice for product shots or text overlays. Zoom in on hair and shoulders before saving; if the edge looks fine there, it looks fine everywhere.

items.steps_title: How to blur background on iPhone in How to Blur Photo

steps.title: Open the app and pick the photo
steps.description: Install How to Blur Photo from the App Store, open it, and choose any photo from your library. Portrait mode is not required — a normal Photo-mode shot works.

steps.title: Stay on the Background tab
steps.description: The Background tab is selected by default. The app finds the subject and masks it so the person or object stays sharp while everything behind them is targeted.

steps.title: Choose a style and set Radius
steps.description: Tap Gaussian for the classic soft look (or Motion, Ghosting, Box, and others). Drag Radius until the background is as blurred as you want; the preview updates live.

steps.title: Save
steps.description: Tap Save in the top-right corner. The edited photo is written to your library as a new image, so the original is untouched.

tips: Photos with clear separation between subject and background (a person against a wall, a cup on a table) mask cleanest.
If a small region near the edge is missed, switch to the Manual tab and brush it yourself before you save.
For action photos, Motion with a low Angle reads as speed rather than as an out-of-focus mistake.

faq.question: Can I blur the background on iPhone without Portrait mode?
faq.answer: Yes. How to Blur Photo separates the subject from the background on any photo, including shots taken in normal Photo mode, older pictures, and images you received from someone else.

faq.question: Can I blur the background on an existing photo in the Photos app?
faq.answer: Only if the photo was captured in Portrait mode. For everything else, Photos has no background-blur control; you need a third-party editor.

faq.question: Which iPhones does the app support?
faq.answer: Any iPhone running iOS 18.6 or later. There is no requirement for Apple Intelligence hardware.

faq.question: Does it upload my photos?
faq.answer: No. The listing states photos are processed on the device and are not uploaded to external servers when you blur backgrounds.

items.intro: “Blur background of photo” is a result people want, not a technique they want to learn: the person or product in front sharp, the clutter behind gone soft. On iPhone that used to mean shooting in Portrait mode or moving the file to a desktop editor. How to Blur Photo does it on the phone, after the shot, with a slider.

native.heading: Before you install anything
paragraphs: Check whether the photo was taken in Portrait mode. If it was, Photos → Edit already lets you change the blur with the f-number control. If the photo was shot in the normal Photo mode, on the selfie camera without Portrait, or it is a screenshot or a saved image, Photos offers no background blur at all — the depth data was never recorded.

sections.heading: What the app does with a background
paragraphs: How to Blur Photo builds a mask around the main subject and applies the blur outside that mask. You can choose the kind of blur: Gaussian for a lens-like softness, Motion for directional streaks, Ghosting for a dreamy double image, Box for a flatter digital look, plus Pixelate, Hexagonal, and Crystallize for stylised backgrounds.
The Radius slider controls strength, and for Motion an Angle slider controls direction. Nothing leaves the phone; the whole pipeline is on-device, which is also why it works without a connection.

sections.heading: Where a blurred background helps most
paragraphs: Profile photos and LinkedIn headshots taken in a kitchen or office. Marketplace product photos where the table and wall distract from the item. Instagram posts where a busy background competes with the person. Group shots where you want attention on one face. In each case the same three taps apply.

items.steps_title: How to blur the background of a photo in the app

steps.title: Choose the photo
steps.description: Open How to Blur Photo and select the image from your library. Any format that Photos can show is fine.

steps.title: Let the Background tab find the subject
steps.description: Background is the default mode. The subject is masked automatically; the preview shows the blur applied only behind it.

steps.title: Set style and strength, then Save

tips: If the app picked the wrong subject in a crowded frame, switch to Manual and brush the areas you want blurred.
Keep Radius below 50 for headshots; strong blur behind a face looks like a cutout.
Save once at a moderate setting and once stronger — it is quicker than second-guessing on a small screen.

items.intro: A blurred photo background is the fastest way to make a phone snapshot look intentional. Feeds are full of Portrait-mode photos, so a flat, everything-in-focus picture stands out for the wrong reason. This guide is about the social-media use case: what strength to use, which style flatters faces, and how to do it on the iPhone in under a minute.
items.image_alt: Profile-style photo with a blurred background created in How to Blur Photo

native.heading: Can Instagram or Photos do this?
paragraphs: Instagram’s editor has no background-blur tool for photos; its blur effects apply to the whole frame or to a radial area. Photos on iPhone only adjusts background blur on Portrait-mode captures. LinkedIn and most dating apps offer no editing at all. So the blur has to happen before you upload, in an editor that understands where the person is.

sections.heading: Which blur style looks right on a face
paragraphs: Gaussian at a moderate Radius is the one that reads as “nice camera”. Bokeh-style softness behind a face is what Portrait mode imitates, and Gaussian gets closest. Motion blur behind a person suggests movement and suits street or gym photos. Ghosting and Crystallize are creative looks for story posts rather than for a profile picture.

For LinkedIn or a CV photo, keep the blur restrained (Radius 30–45) so the setting is still recognisable as an office or outdoors. For Instagram, go heavier (50–70) — feeds are viewed small and subtle blur disappears.

sections.heading: Group photos and multiple people
paragraphs: The Background tab treats detected people as the subject. If you want everyone sharp, that is what you get. If you want only yourself sharp and the rest of the group soft, use the Manual tab and brush over the other people; Radius applies to everything you paint.

items.steps_title: How to blur a photo background for a post

steps.title: Open the photo in How to Blur Photo
steps.description: Pick the picture you plan to post. Selfies, full-length shots, and photos someone else took of you all work.

steps.title: Keep Background selected and choose Gaussian
steps.description: The person is masked automatically. Gaussian gives the portrait-lens look that suits profile pictures.

steps.title: Set Radius for the platform
steps.description: About 40 for LinkedIn or a CV, 50–70 for Instagram and TikTok covers. Zoom in on hair to check the edge.

steps.title: Save and upload
steps.description: Tap Save. The new image is in Recents; upload it from the app of your choice as usual.

tips: Crop after blurring, not before — the subject detector has more context in the full frame.
Avoid maximum Radius on portraits; a face floating on a colour field looks like a cutout.
For a series of posts, use the same Radius on every photo so the feed looks consistent.

faq.question: Does blurring the background reduce photo quality?
faq.answer: The subject keeps its original detail; only the background is processed. The saved copy is a full-resolution image, not a compressed preview.

faq.question: Can I blur the background of a selfie?
faq.answer: Yes. Front-camera photos are handled like any other image; Portrait mode is not required.

faq.question: Can I use it for a LinkedIn or passport-style photo?
faq.answer: For LinkedIn, yes — keep Radius low for a professional look. For passports and official IDs, do not edit the background; those photos must be unretouched.

items.intro: If you have ever looked at a photo and thought “I wish the background was blurry”, this is the guide. It is written for people who are not photographers: no talk of f-stops, just what the options are on an iPhone and which one to use depending on whether the photo already exists.

native.heading: Option 1: before you shoot — Portrait mode
paragraphs: Open Camera, swipe to Portrait, wait for the yellow “Natural Light” label, and take the picture. The background is blurred automatically, and you can adjust the amount later in Photos → Edit with the f-number control. Limitations: you must remember to do it before the shot, the subject has to be within a couple of metres, and it does nothing for photos you already have.

sections.heading: Option 2: after you shoot — How to Blur Photo
paragraphs: For photos that already exist, How to Blur Photo does the job Portrait mode would have done. It finds the subject on its own, and you decide how blurry the background should be with one slider called Radius. There is no masking to learn, and it is free to download for iPhone with iOS 18.6 or later.

What the Radius numbers mean in plain terms: 20–30 is “slightly out of focus”, 40–60 is what most people picture when they say “blurry background”, and 80+ turns the background into soft colour with no detail.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
paragraphs: Blurring the whole photo instead of the background — make sure the Background tab, not Full Photo, is selected. Pushing Radius to the maximum on a portrait — it looks like a sticker. Skipping the zoom check — always pinch in on hair and shoulders before you save.

If you want the background blurry and a face hidden, do the background first, then switch to the Faces tab.

faq.question: Why does Photos not let me blur my background?

items.intro: “How to blur a photo on iPhone” covers two different wishes. Some people want the entire picture soft — for a wallpaper, a story background, or to hide detail. Others want a portrait look where only the background is blurred. The built-in Photos app does neither on a normal photo, so this guide shows both in one app and explains when to use which.
items.image_alt: How to Blur Photo with the Full Photo tab selected and Radius at 79

native.heading: What Photos can and cannot do
paragraphs: Photos → Edit offers exposure, colour, crop, and filters, but no blur slider for a regular photo. The only blur control is the f-number on Portrait-mode captures, and it only affects the background of those specific shots. Markup can cover parts of a picture with shapes, which hides rather than blurs. For any real blur — full image or background — you need a dedicated editor.

sections.heading: Which tab to use
paragraphs: Full Photo: the blur is applied evenly to every pixel. Use it for lock-screen wallpapers, text backgrounds, or when you want to share the mood of a picture without the detail. Background: the app detects the subject and blurs only what is behind it. Use it for portraits, product shots, and anything where a person or object should stand out.
Both tabs share the same style chips — Gaussian, Motion, Ghosting, Box, Pixelate, Hexagonal, Crystallize — and the same Radius slider. Motion adds an Angle slider for direction.

sections.heading: Choosing a style
paragraphs: Gaussian is the neutral, lens-like option and the right default. Ghosting produces a dreamy double image that suits full-photo edits for stories. Motion suggests speed. Pixelate, Box, Hexagonal, and Crystallize are stylised and are better for creative posts or privacy than for realism.

For a portrait, use Background and stay below Radius 60.
If the app detects the wrong subject, the Manual tab lets you brush the blur exactly where you want it.

items.intro: A “picture” on iPhone is often not something you photographed: a screenshot of a chat, an image saved from a website, a photo a friend sent. Those files have no depth data and Photos treats them as flat images, so nothing in the built-in editor will blur them. This guide covers every kind of picture and every kind of blur — the whole thing, the background, or one specific area.

native.heading: What the built-in tools do with a picture
paragraphs: Markup (Photos → Edit → pen icon) can draw shapes and scribbles over a picture, which is a way to hide content but not to blur it. Portrait-mode blur is unavailable on anything that was not captured in Portrait mode, which includes every screenshot and every saved image. The Clean Up tool on Apple Intelligence iPhones removes objects; it is not a blur brush.

sections.heading: Four ways to blur a picture in one app
paragraphs: Full Photo softens the entire picture, which is what you want for a background image or to share a vibe without the detail. Background finds the subject and blurs behind it — this works on saved images too, as long as there is a clear subject. Manual gives you a brush: paint over a name in a screenshot, a house number, or a face in the crowd, and only that area is blurred. Faces detects faces automatically and blurs each one.
All four use the same style chips and the same Radius slider, so once you have done one, you can do the rest.

sections.heading: Screenshots specifically
paragraphs: For screenshots of conversations or documents, the Manual tab with Pixelate or Box is the clearest choice: it makes text unreadable rather than merely soft. Use a Radius high enough that individual letters are not distinguishable when zoomed in, then save and share the copy.

items.intro: Sometimes the goal is the opposite of a sharp photo: a soft, blurry image for a lock screen, a backdrop behind text in a story, an abstract of a sunset, or a way to share a moment without the detail. iPhone’s Photos app cannot do it, and web tools mean uploading the file. How to Blur Photo does it on the phone with one tab and one slider.

native.heading: Is there a built-in way?
paragraphs: No. Photos has no blur filter for a regular image. Some people zoom far into a photo and take a screenshot to get a soft result, which destroys resolution. Others use the Portrait f-number slider, which only works on Portrait captures and only on the background. A dedicated blur tool is the clean way.

sections.heading: Styles that suit a fully blurry photo
paragraphs: Gaussian gives an even, out-of-focus look and is best for wallpapers and text backgrounds. Ghosting overlays a shifted copy of the image for a dreamy, slightly surreal result that works well on landscapes and night shots. Motion turns the frame into streaks and suits lights and cityscapes. Crystallize and Hexagonal make abstract, mosaic-like art from any photo.
Radius controls how far the blur goes. For a wallpaper you want app icons to sit on, 70 or above. For a “soft memory” look where the scene is still recognisable, 25–40.

sections.heading: If you actually want only the background blurry
paragraphs: Many people typing “how to make a photo blurry” mean the portrait effect. If that is you, switch to the Background tab: the subject is kept sharp automatically and the same Radius slider controls the background. The guide on blurring the background on iPhone walks through it.

items.h1: Motion blur effect on iPhone photos — add speed after the shot
items.answer: To add a motion blur effect to a photo on iPhone, open it in How to Blur Photo, keep the Background tab so the subject stays sharp, tap the Motion style, set Radius for the length of the streaks and Angle for their direction, and tap Save. For a full-frame streak, use the Full Photo tab with the same controls.
items.intro: Motion blur is what a camera records when something moves during the exposure: streaks in the direction of travel. Phones freeze motion by default, so action photos often look static. The motion blur effect adds those streaks back — to the background behind a moving subject, or to the whole frame for a panning look — and How to Blur Photo does it on the iPhone with two sliders.
items.image_alt: Motion style selected in How to Blur Photo with Radius and Angle sliders

native.heading: Can iPhone do motion blur natively?
paragraphs: Not on a photo you already took. Some iPhone models offer long-exposure effects on Live Photos, which blur anything that moved during the capture — the opposite of what you usually want, since the subject blurs too. Photos has no directional blur filter. The effect has to be added in an editor that can separate the subject from the background.

sections.heading: Radius and Angle
paragraphs: Radius sets how long the streaks are. Around 30–50 reads as a fast pan; 65 and above (the App Store screenshot shows 65) looks like high speed. Angle sets the direction. Match it to the direction of travel: near 0° for a car crossing the frame, around 90° for a jump or a skateboard trick going up, and something in between for a diagonal.
Because the subject is masked on the Background tab, the person or vehicle stays crisp while the street, track, or crowd streaks behind them — which is exactly how a panned action shot looks.

sections.heading: When to use Full Photo instead
paragraphs: If the whole frame should feel like it is moving — a train window, city lights, a dance floor — switch to the Full Photo tab and apply Motion to everything. Keep Radius lower there; full-frame motion blur becomes abstract quickly.

steps.title: Open the action photo
steps.description: Launch How to Blur Photo and pick the shot — a runner, cyclist, car, pet, or anything with a direction of travel.

steps.description: Drag Radius for streak length and Angle to match the direction of movement. Check the preview at full size.

steps.title: Save
steps.description: Tap Save to export the photo with the motion blur effect.

tips: Angle should follow the subject’s direction, not the camera’s; a runner moving left-to-right wants a horizontal streak.
Slightly lower Radius on the background than you think — a sharp subject in front of moderate streaks reads faster than extreme blur.
Motion also works as a creative background for portraits: try Angle 90° behind a standing person.

faq.question: What is the motion blur effect?
faq.answer: It is directional blur that mimics movement during a camera exposure. Applied behind a sharp subject, it makes a still photo look like a fast pan.

faq.question: Does it work on photos that were not action shots?
faq.answer: Yes. Any photo with a subject can get a motion blur background; it is a popular creative look for portraits and product photos.

items.h1: Gaussian blur on iPhone photos — soft background, sharp subject
items.answer: To apply a gaussian blur on iPhone, open the photo in How to Blur Photo, keep the Background tab so the subject stays sharp (or choose Full Photo to blur everything), tap the Gaussian style, drag Radius to set how soft the result is, and tap Save. Gaussian is the smooth, even blur that most closely resembles a camera lens out of focus.
items.intro: Gaussian blur is the standard soft blur in every image editor: each pixel is averaged with its neighbours using a bell-curve weighting, so the result is smooth with no streaks or blocks. On a photo background it looks like shallow depth of field. This guide explains when to choose Gaussian over other blur types and how to apply it on the iPhone without a desktop app.
items.image_alt: Gaussian style in How to Blur Photo with the background softened

native.heading: Is there a gaussian blur in the Photos app?
paragraphs: No. Photos has no blur filter for a regular photo, gaussian or otherwise. The Portrait f-number control simulates lens blur on Portrait captures only. General photo editors often include a blur tool, but most apply a radial or whole-frame blur rather than detecting the subject for you.

sections.heading: Gaussian vs the other styles
paragraphs: Gaussian is even and directionless — the safe choice for portraits, products, and anything that should look photographic. Box blur is similar but flatter and slightly more digital. Motion adds direction. Ghosting doubles the image. Pixelate, Hexagonal, and Crystallize replace detail with blocks or cells and are stylistic or privacy tools rather than lens simulations.
In How to Blur Photo, Radius maps to the gaussian radius: how many pixels each point is averaged across. Larger radius, softer result.

sections.heading: Typical settings
paragraphs: Headshots: Radius 30–45 keeps the environment readable. Full-length portraits: 45–60. Product photos on a table: 50–70 so the item is the only sharp thing. Full Photo backgrounds for text: 70+.

faq.question: What is gaussian blur?
faq.answer: A smooth blur where each pixel is averaged with its neighbours using a bell-curve weighting. It has no direction and is the closest software match to a lens out of focus.

faq.question: Gaussian blur or bokeh — which should I use for a portrait?

items.h1: Bokeh effect on iPhone — soft, glowing backgrounds on photos you already took
items.answer: To get a bokeh effect on iPhone after the shot, open the photo in How to Blur Photo, keep the Background tab so the subject stays sharp, choose Gaussian for a creamy background or Ghosting for a softer glow, raise Radius until highlights bloom, and tap Save. Portrait mode simulates bokeh only while shooting; this works on any existing photo.
items.intro: Bokeh is the quality of the out-of-focus area in a photo — the soft discs that street lights and sun through leaves turn into behind a portrait. It comes from a wide-aperture lens, which a phone does not have. Portrait mode fakes it at capture time. If the photo is already taken, you can still add the look: this guide shows how, and which style in the app gets closest.
items.image_alt: Ghosting style creating a soft bokeh-like background in How to Blur Photo

native.heading: Bokeh on iPhone without an app
paragraphs: Shoot in Portrait mode and, on supported models, use the f-number slider afterwards to widen the simulated aperture; lower f-numbers give bigger, softer bokeh. Getting physically close to the subject also increases real background blur. Neither helps once a normal photo has been taken, and Photos offers no bokeh filter for existing images.

sections.heading: Which style gives the bokeh look
paragraphs: Gaussian at a higher Radius (55–80) is the closest match to lens bokeh on most backgrounds: highlights soften into glowing patches and colours blend. Ghosting layers a shifted copy of the background, which gives a hazy, romantic glow that suits evening and backlit photos — the App Store listing calls it “soft vibes with bokeh”. Pick Gaussian for realism and Ghosting for mood.
The subject is masked automatically on the Background tab, so the person stays crisp while the background blooms. That contrast is what makes bokeh read as bokeh.

sections.heading: Photos that suit the effect
paragraphs: Backgrounds with point lights — fairy lights, city streets at night, sun through trees — produce the classic discs. Plain walls become smooth gradients, which still isolates the subject but looks less dramatic. A little distance between subject and background makes the result more believable.

tips: Slightly underexposed backgrounds with bright points give the most convincing bokeh.
Do not push Radius past the point where the subject’s edge starts to glow; step back a little.
For group photos where only one person should be sharp, use the Manual tab and brush over the others.

faq.question: Can I add bokeh to a photo after taking it on iPhone?
faq.answer: Yes. How to Blur Photo keeps the subject sharp and softens the background with Gaussian or Ghosting, which produces the bokeh look on any existing photo.

faq.question: What is the difference between bokeh and background blur?
faq.answer: Background blur is the general effect; bokeh describes the character of that blur, especially how highlights render. Strong, smooth background blur with glowing highlights is what people mean by a bokeh effect.

faq.question: Does it need Portrait mode or a Pro iPhone?

items.h1: How to blur faces in a photo on iPhone
items.answer: To blur faces in a photo on iPhone, open it in How to Blur Photo, tap the Faces tab, and the app detects every face and blurs each one; set Radius for how strong the blur is, choose Pixelate or Gaussian, and tap Save. It works on any iPhone running iOS 18.6 or later, without Apple Intelligence, and the photo never leaves the device.
items.intro: Blurring faces is the polite default before posting a group photo, a class picture, a protest, or a street scene: not everyone in the frame agreed to be online. iPhones with Apple Intelligence gained a way to do this in Photos, but it is limited to recent Pro and 16-series models and certain regions. This guide covers the built-in option, its limits, and a way that works on every supported iPhone.
items.image_alt: Grid of detected faces, each blurred, in How to Blur Photo

native.heading: What the Photos app offers
paragraphs: On iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 16 and newer models running iOS 18.1 or later with Apple Intelligence enabled, Photos → Edit → Clean Up lets you brush over a face; the tool pixelates or blurs the covered area. It is manual (one face at a time), the strength is not adjustable, and it is unavailable on older iPhones and in some regions and languages. Without Apple Intelligence, Photos can only cover a face with a Markup shape or sticker — hiding, not blurring.

sections.heading: Automatic face blur for every supported iPhone
paragraphs: How to Blur Photo has a dedicated Faces tab. It detects the faces in the frame and shows them in a grid, each already blurred, so a group photo with a dozen people takes one tap rather than a dozen brush strokes. You choose the style — Pixelate for the classic censored look, Gaussian or Box for a softer one — and Radius for how strong it is. Processing is on-device, which matters when the whole point is privacy.
The requirement is iOS 18.6 or later on any iPhone; there is no dependency on Apple Intelligence hardware.

sections.heading: Blur some faces, keep others
paragraphs: If you want your own face visible and everyone else blurred, use the Manual tab after or instead of Faces: brush over the faces you want hidden and leave yours alone. The same Radius and style apply to the painted area.

sections.heading: How strong is strong enough
paragraphs: A face is still recognisable at low blur, especially to people who know the person. For genuine anonymity, use Pixelate or a Gaussian Radius high enough that eyes, nose, and mouth are indistinguishable at full zoom. The App Store screenshot shows Radius 80 for faces; treat that as a sensible starting point, not a maximum.

faq.question: Is blurring faces reversible by someone else?
faq.answer: A strong Pixelate or high-Radius Gaussian removes the underlying detail from the saved copy. Do not share the original, and use a strength that makes features indistinguishable at full zoom.

items.h1: How to blur part of a picture on iPhone
items.answer: To blur part of a picture on iPhone, open it in How to Blur Photo, tap the Manual tab, brush with your finger over the area you want hidden, choose Pixelate or Gaussian, drag Radius until the detail is unreadable, and tap Save. The iPhone Photos app has no blur brush; Markup can only cover an area with a solid shape.
items.intro: The most common “blur” question on Apple’s own forums is about blurring a specific part of a picture: an address in a screenshot, a stranger in the background, a credit card on a table, a child’s school badge. Photos cannot do it — Markup draws shapes, and Clean Up (on Apple Intelligence iPhones) is designed to remove objects, not blur them. Here is what actually works, using the Manual mode in How to Blur Photo.
items.image_alt: Manual tab in How to Blur Photo used to blur a chosen region

native.heading: The built-in workarounds and their limits
paragraphs: Markup (Photos → Edit → pen icon → + → Add Shape) places a filled rectangle or circle over the area. It hides the content, but it looks like a censor bar and, if you use the highlighter or a low-opacity shape, the detail underneath can still be read. On Apple Intelligence iPhones, Clean Up removes what you brush over, which can leave odd artefacts and does not work on older devices. Neither gives you an actual blur with adjustable strength.

sections.heading: Manual mode: a blur brush for any region
paragraphs: How to Blur Photo’s Manual tab turns your finger into a blur brush. Paint over the region; only the painted area is affected. The style chips decide what kind of blur — Pixelate and Box make text unreadable with a clean, deliberate look; Gaussian gives a soft blur that suits faces and objects; Crystallize and Hexagonal are stylised. Radius controls strength, and the live preview shows exactly what will be saved.
Because you are painting rather than selecting, irregular shapes are easy: a licence plate at an angle, a name badge, a reflection in a window.

sections.heading: Screenshots, documents, and chats
paragraphs: For text, use Pixelate or Box with a Radius high enough that letters are not distinguishable when you zoom in. For a person or object in the background, Gaussian at a moderate Radius looks more natural. In both cases, zoom in before saving — a blur that looks sufficient at thumbnail size is often still readable at full size.

items.answer: To blur text in a photo on iPhone, open the image in How to Blur Photo, tap Manual, brush over the text, choose Pixelate (or Box), raise Radius until individual letters cannot be distinguished when zoomed in, and tap Save. Do not rely on a light blur or a Markup highlighter — both can leave text readable.
items.intro: Sharing a screenshot of an order confirmation, a group chat, a ticket, or a document almost always means hiding some text first: a full name, an address, a booking reference, a phone number. Doing it properly matters because a weak blur can be read or even reconstructed. This guide shows the right way on iPhone and the settings that make text unrecoverable.
items.image_alt: Manual tab with Pixelate style hiding text in How to Blur Photo

native.heading: Why Markup is not enough
paragraphs: Markup’s pen and highlighter are semi-transparent by default, and people regularly share screenshots where the “hidden” text is legible through the stroke. A solid Markup shape at full opacity does hide text, but it looks like a redaction bar and has to be drawn and resized for each line. Clean Up on Apple Intelligence iPhones is built for objects and can produce garbled text rather than removing it.

sections.heading: Pixelate versus blur for text
paragraphs: For text, Pixelate is the better choice. It replaces the area with large blocks, so there is no residual shape to reconstruct, and it visibly communicates “this was hidden on purpose”. Box blur is a close second. Gaussian at a very high Radius also works but needs to be pushed further than people expect; at low Radius the word shapes remain readable. In every case, zoom in before saving.
Radius controls block size for Pixelate. Choose a value where a single block is larger than a letter — for typical screenshot text that means well above 50.

sections.heading: Whole screenshots and multiple lines
paragraphs: If most of a screenshot needs hiding, the Full Photo tab with Pixelate obscures everything, and you can crop afterwards to keep only the relevant part. For a few scattered lines, Manual with a wide brush stroke per line is quicker than shapes in Markup.

tips: Hide the text before you crop; cropping first can leave part of a line at the edge.
Look for the same information elsewhere in the screenshot — URL bars, notification banners, and app headers often repeat a name or email.
Share the exported copy, not the original; the original still contains the text.

faq.answer: Light gaussian blur on text can sometimes be reconstructed. Pixelate with blocks larger than a letter, or a very high Radius, removes the information from the saved image. Never share the original.

items.answer: To blur a license plate in a photo on iPhone, open the image in How to Blur Photo, tap Manual, brush over the plate, choose Pixelate or Box, raise Radius until the characters cannot be read, and tap Save. It takes under a minute per photo and the image never leaves your iPhone.
items.intro: Car listings, road-trip albums, dashcam stills, and parking disputes all end up online with plates visible. A plate ties a photo to a registered address and is routinely scraped from marketplaces. Blurring it before upload is quick on iPhone once you have a tool with a brush — the Photos app itself does not have one.
items.image_alt: Manual blur over a number plate in How to Blur Photo

native.heading: Built-in options
paragraphs: Markup can place a solid rectangle over the plate (Photos → Edit → pen → + → Add Shape → fill). It works, but it looks like a black bar, needs rotating to match an angled plate, and is easy to leave semi-transparent by mistake. Clean Up on Apple Intelligence iPhones may try to remove the plate and generate a blank bumper, with mixed results. A blur brush is simpler and looks like a normal edited photo.

sections.heading: Pixelate or Box for plates
paragraphs: Plates are high-contrast text, and high-contrast text is the easiest thing to reconstruct from a weak blur. Pixelate at a Radius where each block is larger than a character is the safe choice and is what news outlets use. Box blur at a high Radius is a softer-looking alternative. Gaussian works only if pushed very high; at moderate settings the letter shapes survive.
For a car listing, blur the plate on every photo in the set, including reflections in bumpers, windows, and wet ground behind the car.

sections.heading: Angled plates and multiple cars
paragraphs: Because Manual mode is a brush rather than a rectangle, an angled or partly obscured plate is painted in one stroke. In a car-park photo with several vehicles, paint each plate; Radius applies to all of them at once.

faq.question: Which blur style is safest for plates?

items.h1: How to pixelate a photo on iPhone — faces, text, or the whole image
items.answer: To pixelate a photo on iPhone, open it in How to Blur Photo, choose a tab — Faces to pixelate detected faces automatically, Manual to brush over text or an object, Background or Full Photo for larger areas — tap the Pixelate style, drag Radius to set the block size, and tap Save. The Photos app has no pixelate tool for regular photos.
items.intro: Pixelation replaces an area with large square blocks. It is the standard way to hide identity or text because it is obvious, clean, and, done properly, irreversible. It is also a look in its own right — retro, 8-bit, glitchy. On iPhone the Photos app cannot pixelate a normal photo; How to Blur Photo makes it a style you can apply to faces, a brushed region, the background, or the whole frame.
items.image_alt: Pixelate and Crystallize style chips in How to Blur Photo

native.heading: Pixelate in Photos?
paragraphs: Only via Clean Up on iPhones with Apple Intelligence (iPhone 15 Pro, 16-series and newer, iOS 18.1+), which pixelates or blurs a brushed face with a fixed strength. On other iPhones, and for text or whole-image pixelation, Photos has nothing. Markup shapes cover rather than pixelate.

sections.heading: Block size and Radius
paragraphs: In How to Blur Photo, Radius controls the size of the pixel blocks. Small values give a fine mosaic that hides detail while keeping the general shape; large values give big, obvious squares. For privacy on faces and text, use a block size larger than an eye or a letter. For a retro look on the whole photo, a medium value keeps the scene recognisable.
Pixelate is one of the style chips next to Gaussian, Motion, Ghosting, Box, Hexagonal, and Crystallize. Hexagonal is the same idea with hex cells; Crystallize uses irregular shards.

sections.heading: Four places to pixelate
paragraphs: Faces tab: every detected face is pixelated at once — the App Store listing calls it “pixel privacy in one tap”. Manual tab: brush over a plate, a badge, a screen, or text. Background tab: keep the subject sharp and pixelate everything behind them for a stylised portrait. Full Photo: pixelate the entire image for an abstract or 8-bit version.

items.steps_title: How to pixelate a photo in How to Blur Photo

steps.title: Open the photo
steps.description: Launch How to Blur Photo and choose the image.

steps.title: Choose where to pixelate
steps.description: Faces for people, Manual to brush an area, Background or Full Photo for larger regions.

steps.title: Tap Pixelate and drag Radius
steps.description: Pixelate is in the style row. Increase Radius until blocks are large enough to hide detail.

steps.title: Save
steps.description: Zoom in to check, then tap Save to export the pixelated photo.

tips: For privacy, err on the side of larger blocks; small pixelation on faces is surprisingly recognisable.
For an 8-bit look, use Full Photo with a medium Radius on a high-contrast image.
Hexagonal and Crystallize give a similar privacy result with a more decorative pattern.

faq.question: How do I pixelate a face on iPhone?
faq.answer: Open the photo in How to Blur Photo, tap Faces, tap Pixelate, raise Radius, and Save. All detected faces are pixelated together.

faq.question: Can pixelated photos be reversed?
faq.answer: Not when the blocks are larger than the features they cover; the detail is discarded in the saved copy. Keep the original private.

faq.question: Is there a free pixelate app for iPhone?
faq.answer: How to Blur Photo is free to download and includes Pixelate as a style; advanced options are optional in-app purchases.

items.cta_body: Download How to Blur Photo, choose Faces or Manual, tap Pixelate. Free to install, on-device, iPhone with iOS 18.6 or later.

items.h1: Best app to blur background on iPhone — what to use when the photo is already taken
items.answer: The best app to blur the background on iPhone depends on when you need it: Portrait mode is best before the shot; for photos you already have, a dedicated subject-aware editor such as How to Blur Photo is the practical choice — automatic subject detection, adjustable strength, face and manual modes, free to download, and processed on-device. Markup, Clean Up, and browser tools each solve a different, narrower problem.
items.intro: “Best app to blur background on iPhone” usually returns a list of ten general photo editors. Most people asking do not want ten editors; they want to know which route gets a sharp subject and a soft background on a photo that is already in their library, without a learning curve or an upload. This page compares the real options — including the ones built into iOS — against that job.
items.image_alt: How to Blur Photo — sharp subject, blurred background

native.heading: Built-in options first
paragraphs: Portrait mode (Camera): best quality when it works, but only at capture time, only within a couple of metres, and useless for existing photos. Photos f-number slider: adjusts blur on Portrait captures only. Markup: covers areas with shapes; no blur. Clean Up: on Apple Intelligence iPhones, removes objects and can pixelate a brushed face; it does not blur a background. If your photo is already taken in normal mode, none of these blur its background.

sections.heading: What to look for in a background blur app
paragraphs: Automatic subject detection, so you are not tracing outlines with a finger. Adjustable strength, because a headshot and a product photo need different amounts. A manual brush for the cases detection misses. Privacy options (face blur) in the same tool, since the same photos often need both. On-device processing, so personal photos are not uploaded to a server. A price you can see up front.
Web-based blur tools tick some of these boxes but require uploading the photo and typically export a compressed or watermarked file on the free tier.

sections.heading: How to Blur Photo against that list
paragraphs: How to Blur Photo (published under the Make Blur brand) is built around this one job. It detects the subject on the Background tab, has a Radius slider for strength, a Manual tab with a brush, a Faces tab for privacy, and a Full Photo tab. Styles include Gaussian, Motion, Ghosting, Box, Pixelate, Hexagonal, and Crystallize. Processing is on-device with no internet required. It is free to download on iPhone with iOS 18.6 or later; basic background blur is included and advanced styles and tools are optional in-app purchases.

What it is not: a general photo editor, a background remover (no transparent cutouts), or a video tool. If you need those, a broader app is the better choice; if you need the background of a photo blurred today, this one is quicker.

steps.title: Install from the App Store
steps.description: Search for How to Blur Photo or use the download button on this page. Free to install.

steps.title: Open a photo with a busy background
steps.description: The Background tab detects the subject. Pick Gaussian and drag Radius.

steps.title: Save and compare
steps.description: Tap Save and look at the original and the edit side by side in Photos.

tips: Photo not taken yet → use Portrait mode.
Photo already taken, need a blurred background or a hidden face → How to Blur Photo.
Need a transparent cutout or video blur → a different category of app.

faq.question: Can the iPhone blur the background of a photo by itself?
faq.answer: Only for photos captured in Portrait mode. For normal photos, screenshots, and received images, iOS has no background-blur tool.

faq.question: Do I need a Pro iPhone or Apple Intelligence?
faq.answer: No. The app runs on any iPhone with iOS 18.6 or later.
